## Q1
Which of the following is not an interprocess communication mechanism in UNIX?

## Q1 - Options
(A) Pipes
(B) Messages
(C) Shared memory
(D) Semaphore

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q76

Pipes, message queues, and shared memory transfer information between processes. A semaphore is principally a synchronization primitive: it coordinates access rather than carrying a message payload.

## Q3
Once a process is executing, which events could not occur: issuing I/O then joining the ready queue; creating a child and waiting for it; time-slice expiry then joining the waiting queue; or interrupt-driven removal then joining the waiting queue?

## Q3 - Options
(A) B only
(B) D only
(C) A and C only
(D) A, C, and D only

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q62

An I/O request blocks the process, sending it to waiting rather than ready. Expiry of a time slice preempts it to ready, not waiting. An interrupt can also preempt it to ready; it does not by itself make the process wait. Waiting for a child is a valid blocking event, so A, C, and D are the impossible descriptions.

## Q4
Which statement about spinlock semaphores is correct?

## Q4 - Options
(A) They are busy-waiting semaphores.
(B) They are not useful when locks are held briefly.
(C) Waiting for one may require multiple context switches.
(D) They are often employed on uniprocessor systems.

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q63

A spinlock repeatedly tests a lock while busy waiting. It is useful for very short critical sections because it can avoid sleep-and-wakeup overhead; waiting does not itself cause context switches, and spinning is generally unsuitable on a uniprocessor because the lock holder needs CPU time to run.

## Q5
Which of the following statements are TRUE about mutual exclusion in concurrent programming ?<br>
A. Mutual exclusion ensures that only one process can be in a critical section at any given time.<br>
B. Mutual exclusion are designed to prevent conflicts and ensure that only one process can access shared resources at a time.<br>
C. Mutual exclusion can use various algorithms to ensure that processes do not enter the critical section simultaneously.<br>
D. Mutual exclusion allows multiple processes to access the critical section simultaneously to improve performance.

## Q5 - Options
(A) (A), (B), (C) Only
(B) (B), (C), (D) Only
(C) (B), (D), (A) Only
(D) (A), (C), (D) Only

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q5

Statements (A), (B) and (C) all restate the same guarantee — at most one process inside the critical section at a time, enforced by locks or algorithms such as Peterson’s. (D) contradicts the definition outright, since allowing simultaneous access is exactly what mutual exclusion prevents. Only (A), (B) and (C), so option A is correct.

**Answer:** C

**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q75

## Q9
At a particular time of computation, the value of a counting semaphore is 7. Then 20 P operations and x V operations were completed on this semaphore. If the final value of the semaphore is 5, x will be

## Q9 - Options
(A) 15
(B) 22
(C) 18
(D) 13

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q18

Each P operation decrements a counting semaphore by 1 and each V operation increments it by 1, so the final value equals the initial value minus the number of P operations plus the number of V operations.

Final value = 7 − 20 + x = 5.

Solving gives x = 5 − 7 + 20 = 18.

- **A. 15**, **B. 22**, and **D. 13** — these do not satisfy 7 − 20 + x = 5 and come from arithmetic errors in isolating x.
- **C. 18** — correct, since 7 − 20 + 18 = 5.

## Q10
Match List I with List II on operating system synchronization concepts.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Critical region | I. Hoare's monitor |
| B. Wait signal | II. Mutual exclusion |
| C. Working set | III. Principle of locality |
| D. Deadlock | IV. Circular wait |

List I / List II: operating system synchronization and memory concepts

## Q10 - Options
(A) A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II
(B) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
(C) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(D) A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q69

Each operating-system term matches a distinct named concept.

- A critical region is the mechanism operating systems use to enforce mutual exclusion over shared resources — A-II.
- The wait and signal operations are the two primitive operations defined in Hoare's monitor construct for process synchronization — B-I.
- The working set model is built directly on the principle of locality of reference, tracking the pages a process has referenced recently — C-III.
- Circular wait is one of the four Coffman conditions necessary for deadlock — D-IV.

This gives the mapping A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

- **A. A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II** — swaps A and D's correct pairings.
- **B. A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV** — correct, matches every pairing above.
- **C. A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV** — swaps A and B's correct pairings.
- **D. A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II** — misassigns three of the four pairings.

## Q11
Assertion (A): A process involves a library function to create a thread.<br>
Reason (R): The threads make system calls to convey their resource and I/O requirement to the Kernel.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

## Q11 - Options
(A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
(B) Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(C) A is true but R is false
(D) A is false but R is true

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q90

Assertion A is true. Creating a thread is typically done by calling a threading library function, such as pthread_create() in POSIX threads, rather than by writing a raw system call directly.

Reason R is also true on its own. Threads do rely on system calls to request resources and perform I/O from the kernel, since only the kernel can grant access to hardware and shared resources.

However, R does not explain A. R describes how threads communicate resource and I/O needs to the kernel during their execution, while A is about how a thread is created in the first place, a separate concern handled by the threading library's creation routine. So both statements are true, but R is not the reason A is true.

## Q12
Process in memory also contain the heap section. What is the use of heap section?

## Q12 - Options
(A) Contains temporary data
(B) Dynamically allocate the memory during process run time
(C) Contains Process priority and pointers to scheduling queues
(D) Contains amount of CPU and real time use

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q18

The heap is the memory region a process uses for dynamic memory allocation requested during execution, such as through malloc in C or new in C++, and it grows and shrinks as the program allocates and frees memory at runtime.

This makes option B the correct description, since "temporary data" describes the stack (used for local variables and function calls), while process priority and CPU/real-time usage information are stored in the process control block, not the heap.

## Q13
Degree of concurrency in thread can be arranged in the manner.

## Q13 - Options
(A) one-to-one &gt; many-to-one &gt; many-to-many
(B) one-to-one &gt; many-to-many &gt; many-to-one
(C) many-to-many &gt; many-to-one &gt; one-to-one
(D) None of the above

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q20

The degree of concurrency a threading model achieves depends on how many kernel threads can actually run in parallel on available processors.

In the many-to-one model, all user threads map to a single kernel thread, so only one thread can be scheduled on a CPU at a time, giving the least concurrency of the three.

The one-to-one model maps each user thread to its own kernel thread, letting the kernel schedule several threads on multiple processors truly in parallel, which is commonly presented as offering the greatest concurrency.

The many-to-many model sits between the two, multiplexing many user threads onto a smaller or equal pool of kernel threads, which allows some but not full parallel scheduling.

This ranking, one-to-one above many-to-many above many-to-one, matches option B. Note that some operating-systems texts treat many-to-many as offering concurrency comparable to one-to-one since it can also scale kernel threads to the processor count, so this specific ranking should be spot-checked against the exact course reference in use.

## Q14
In design protocol of critical section problem, each process must ask permission to enter critical section in \_\_\_\_ code, it then executes in the critical section, once it finishes executing in the critical section it enters the \_\_\_\_ code. The process then enters the \_\_\_\_ code.

## Q14 - Options
(A) entry section, remainder section, exit section
(B) entry section, exit section, remainder section
(C) remainder section, entry section, exit section
(D) remainder section, exit section, entry section

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q52

The critical section protocol cycles through three named regions of code in a fixed order.

A process first requests permission in the entry section, runs its critical section code, then releases access in the exit section, and finally does unrelated work in the remainder section before looping back to the entry section again.

## Q16
If an operating system does not allow a child process to exist when the parent process has been terminated, this phenomenon is called as -

## Q16 - Options
(A) Threading
(B) Cascading termination
(C) Zombie termination
(D) Process killing

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q22

When an operating system's policy forces every child process to be terminated as soon as its parent terminates, so that termination propagates down the process tree, this is called cascading termination. It is a deliberate OS design choice, not the same as a zombie process, which is a terminated process whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent.

## Q20
Which of the following interprocess communication model is used to exchange messages among co-operative processes?

## Q20 - Options
(A) Shared memory model
(B) Message passing model
(C) Shared memory and message passing model
(D) Queues

## Q20 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q71

Operating systems provide two fundamental interprocess communication models for cooperating processes:

1. Shared Memory Model — cooperating processes establish a mapped memory region that multiple processes can read and write directly.
2. Message Passing Model — processes communicate without sharing address space by exchanging messages via system calls managed by the kernel.

Both models are standard mechanisms used to exchange messages and synchronize cooperative processes.

## Q21
At a particular time of computation, the value of a counting semaphore is 7. Then 20 P (wait) operations and 15 V (signal) operations are completed on this semaphore. What is the resulting value of the semaphore?

## Q21 - Options
(A) 28
(B) 12
(C) 2
(D) 42

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q49

Counting semaphores modify their counter value according to the completed synchronization primitives:

- Each P (wait) operation decrements the semaphore counter by 1.
- Each V (signal) operation increments the semaphore counter by 1.

Initial value = 7.<br>
Net change = -20 (from P operations) + 15 (from V operations) = -5.

Final semaphore value = 7 - 5 = 2.

## Q22
Which of the following are NOT shared by the threads of the same process?<br>
(a) Stack<br>
(b) Registers<br>
(c) Address space<br>
(d) Message queue

## Q22 - Options
(A) (a) and (d)
(B) (b) and (c)
(C) (a) and (b)
(D) (a), (b) and (c)

## Q22 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q90

Thread-level resource isolation versus sharing in multithreaded systems:

Threads within the same process share common process resources:

- Address space (c)
- Global variables and static memory
- Operating system resources such as open file descriptors and IPC message queues (d)

Each thread maintains its own private execution state:

- Stack (a) for local activation frames and function calls
- Register set (b) including the program counter and stack pointer

Thus, stack and registers are not shared across threads.

## Q23
Suppose P, Q and R are co-operating processes satisfying Mutual Exclusion condition. Then, if the process Q is executing in its critical section then

## Q23 - Options
(A) Both ‘P’ and ‘R’ execute in critical section.
(B) ‘R’ executes in critical section.
(C) ‘P’ executes in critical section.
(D) Neither ‘P’ nor ‘R’ executes in their critical section.

## Q23 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q42

Mutual exclusion strictly guarantees that no more than one process can execute inside its critical section concurrently.

- If process Q is currently executing in its critical section, any other cooperating process (P or R) attempting to enter must be blocked until Q leaves.
- Therefore, neither P nor R can execute in their critical section simultaneously (Option D).
- Options A, B, and C directly violate the mutual exclusion condition.

## Q25
To overcome difficulties in Readers–Writers problem, which of the following statement/s is/are true ?

(i) Writers are given exclusive access to shared objects.<br>
(ii) Readers are given exclusive access to shared objects.<br>
(iii) Both Readers and Writers are given exclusive access to shared objects.

Choose the correct answer from the code given below :<br>
Code :

## Q25 - Options
(A) Both (ii) and (iii)
(B) (iii) only
(C) (i) only
(D) (ii) only

## Q25 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Process Management, IPC, Semaphores & Threads
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q90

In concurrency control for the Readers-Writers problem, writers require exclusive access while readers share concurrent access.

- Multiple reader processes may concurrently read shared data without causing race conditions or data inconsistency.
- Writers modify shared records, so write operations require mutual exclusion from all other readers and all other writers to prevent dirty reads and corrupted writes.
- Giving readers exclusive access (statements ii and iii) unnecessarily serializes read operations and contradicts the fundamental design of the Readers-Writers synchronization protocol.
- Therefore, only statement (i) is true (Option C).
